136450.title: DRA: support non-pod references in ReservedFor
136450.description: TheResourceClaim controller would fail to process and clean up stale pod references if it encountered any non-pod references in the status.reservedFor field. This halted the controller's operation, preventing necessary cleanup.

136509.title: client-go informers: fix potential deadlock
136509.description:
In the unlikely situation that sharedProcessor.distribute was triggered by a resync before sharedProcessor.run had a chance to start the listeners, the sharedProcessor deadlocked: sharedProcessor.distribute held a read/write lock on listenersLock while being blocked on the write to the listener's channel. The listeners who would have read from those weren't get started because sharedProcessor.run was blocked trying to get a read lock for listenersLock.

This gets fixed by releasing the read/write lock in sharedProcessor.distribute while waiting for all listeners to be started. Because either all or no listeners are started, the existing global listenersStarted boolean is sufficient.

The TestListenerResyncPeriods tests now runs twice, with and without the artificial delay. It gets converted to a synctest, so it executes quickly despite the time.Sleep calls and timing is deterministic. The enhanced log output confirms that with the delay, the initial sync completes later:

136027.title: Error-level logs incorrectly use verbosity levels
136027.description:
Currently, some components in Kubernetes have been migrated (or partially migrated) to contextual logging. However, an incorrect pattern was introduced during the migration: Error-level logs are being called with verbosity methods (e.g., .V()).

The underlying package go-logr/logr, which contextual logging relies on, ignores the verbosity level when printing Error-level logs. For example, in the statement logger.V(8).Error(nil, "Readiness probe already exists for container", "pod", klog.KObj(pod), "containerName", c.Name), the error log will be printed regardless of the verbosity level set.

This can lead to error log flooding, which may hinder users' ability to review normal logs for troubleshooting. More critically, according to the Kubernetes logging policy, logs should only be recorded when the information requires action from an administrator. This directly contradicts the practice of setting verbosity levels for Error logs, as administrators using the default logging level might miss these actionable errors. Therefore, these instances need to be fixed.

Using grep, I identified the following instances in the k/k repository where verbosity levels are incorrectly set for Error logs.

3269.title: kubeadm should confirm that the new etcd peer has started before trying to promote it to a member, and even remove the unstarted peer
3269.description:
What would you like to be added?
I think kubeadm should confirm that the new etcd peer has started. If it is has not (e.g. because the etcd image is unavailable, or kubelet has stopped), then kubeadm should not try to promote it to a member, and should eventually remove the member.

Why is this needed?
When kubeadm joins a control plane node with local etcd, it

Makes an etcd API call to add a new etcd peer as a learner.
Creates the etcd static pod
Makes an API call to promote the learner to a member
For (3) to complete, the etcd peer must be started.

If it is not started, then (3) eventually fails, and kubeadm just returns the etcd API call error: can only promote a learner member which is in sync with leader. This error is ambiguous, because it can have other causes, like poor disk/network performance.

Moreover, if the etcd peer never started, then it can safely be removed from the membership list, and kubeadm should do that.

135835.title: Slow pod scheduling when ResourceClaimTemplate is created after pod creation due to exponential backoff
135835.description:
What happened?
When a Pod references a ResourceClaimTemplate (RCT) that doesn't exist at pod creation time, and the RCT is created later, there can be significant delays before the pod gets scheduled.

Root Cause:

The ResourceClaim controller in kube-controller-manager uses AddRateLimited() when the referenced ResourceClaimTemplate is not found. This applies dual rate limiting:

Exponential backoff (per-item): 5ms × 2^failures, capped at 1000 seconds
Token bucket (global): 10 QPS with 100-token burst
The final delay is MAX(exponential_delay, token_bucket_delay).

The Problem:

When the ResourceClaimTemplate is eventually created, there is no mechanism to:

Notify the ResourceClaim controller to immediately reprocess waiting pods
Move affected pods from unschedulablePods queue back to activeQ in the scheduler
The pod must wait for its current backoff period to expire before the controller retries, which can be up to 1000 seconds if the pod has already failed multiple times.

What did you expect to happen?
When a new ResourceClaimTemplate is created, pods that were waiting due to the missing template should be processed promptly (within seconds), not after potentially long backoff delays.

How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Create a Pod that references a non-existent ResourceClaimTemplate:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: nginx
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: my-claim
  resourceClaims:
  - name: my-claim
    resourceClaimTemplateName: my-template  # Does not exist yet
Wait for several retry cycles (observe increasing backoff delays in controller logs)
Create the ResourceClaimTemplate:
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: my-template
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: device
        deviceClassName: example-class

132333.title: scheduler_unschedulable_pods metric might broke when running PreEnqueue plugins
132333.description:
What happened?
scheduler_unschedulable_pods metric stores the number of unschedulable pods broken down by plugin name. It is incremented when the pod is re-added to the scheduling queue (with its all unschedulable and pending plugins) as well as when PreEnqueue plugin fails for such pod. When the pod is popped out from the scheduling queue, the metric is decremented using pod's unschedulable and pending pods lists. However, if PreEnqueue fails for a plugin that was already reported as unschedulable for a pod, the metric is still incremented (multiple ones for one plugin and one pod) what leads to not clearing the metric properly when popping out the pod.

What did you expect to happen?
scheduler_unschedulable_pods metric to be incremented properly when PreEnqueue fails.

How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Create a pod that will get rejected by a plugin while scheduling (e.g. on Filter) and then blocked by PreEnqueue by the same plugin. If the pod is finally scheduled, the scheduler_unschedulable_pods will be non-zero.
